tool.name: Maven
tool.tagline: Convention-driven build and dependency manager for Java projects, defined by the POM
tool.description: Apache Maven builds Java projects from a declarative pom.xml: it resolves dependencies from Maven Central, runs a fixed lifecycle of phases (compile, test, package, install, deploy) through plugins, and defines the repository format the whole JVM ecosystem shares. Knowing it lets you build and maintain the many Java codebases, including most Spring Boot services, that use it.

concepts.name: The POM and the mvn command
concepts.summary: Read a minimal pom.xml, understand coordinates and packaging, and run the common mvn commands.
concepts.why: The POM is the single source of truth for a Maven build; every task starts from it and from the mvn command.
concepts.body:
Maven describes a project in `pom.xml`, the **Project Object Model**. Every project has **coordinates**:

- `groupId`: the organization or project namespace, like `com.acme`.
- `artifactId`: the name of the module, like `shop-api`.
- `version`: `1.0.0` for a release or `1.1.0-SNAPSHOT` for work in progress.
- `packaging`: `jar` (default), `war`, or `pom` for aggregator/parent projects.

The same coordinates identify every library you depend on. Maven follows **convention over configuration**: sources live in `src/main/java`, resources in `src/main/resources`, tests in `src/test/java`, and output goes to `target/`. You configure only what differs from the conventions.

Set the Java version with the `maven.compiler.release` property (`<properties><maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release></properties>`), and `project.build.sourceEncoding` to `UTF-8`.

Common commands:

- `mvn compile`, `mvn test`, `mvn package` (builds `target/shop-api-1.0.0.jar`), `mvn verify`, `mvn install` (copies to `~/.m2/repository`).
- `mvn clean` deletes `target/`; `mvn clean package` is the typical full build.
- `-q` quiet, `-X` debug, `-e` show stack traces, `-DskipTests` skip tests, `-o` offline, `-f other/pom.xml` another file.

Most projects commit the **Maven Wrapper** (`mvnw`, `.mvn/wrapper/`) created with `mvn wrapper:wrapper`, so everyone uses the same Maven version; run `./mvnw` instead of `mvn`.
concepts.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop-api</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>
</project>

<!-- src/main/java/com/acme/App.java, then:
     ./mvnw clean package        -> target/shop-api-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
     ./mvnw test -q              -> runs src/test/java with Surefire
     java -cp target/classes com.acme.App -->
takeaways: groupId:artifactId:version identify a project and every dependency
Conventions: src/main/java, src/test/java, target/
maven.compiler.release sets the Java version
clean, compile, test, package, install are the everyday commands
pitfalls: Running mvn with a different major version than teammates; commit the wrapper and use ./mvnw.

quiz.q: What does mvn install do beyond mvn package?
options: Copies the built artifact into the local repository (~/.m2) so other local projects can depend on it
quiz.explain: install runs package and then places the artifact and POM in the local repository.

concepts.name: Declaring dependencies and scopes
concepts.summary: Add libraries with dependency elements and the compile, provided, runtime, test and import scopes.
concepts.why: Scopes decide what ends up on the compile classpath and in your packaged artifact.
concepts.body:
Dependencies are listed under `<dependencies>`, each with coordinates and an optional **scope**:

- `compile` (default): needed to compile, test and run; propagates to consumers of your artifact.
- `provided`: needed to compile but supplied at run time by the container or platform (servlet API, Lombok, annotation processors). Not packaged, not transitive.
- `runtime`: not needed to compile, needed to run and test (JDBC drivers, logging implementations).
- `test`: only for compiling and running tests (JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ).
- `import`: only in `dependencyManagement`, to import a BOM (next lessons).
- `system` is deprecated; avoid it.

Maven downloads artifacts from **Maven Central** by default (plus any `<repositories>` you add) into the local repository `~/.m2/repository`, which is shared by all your projects. `mvn dependency:tree` prints the resolved graph, `mvn dependency:analyze` flags used-but-undeclared and declared-but-unused dependencies, and `mvn dependency:resolve -U` forces a re-check of snapshots.

**Transitive** dependencies are included automatically with scopes adjusted: a `compile` dependency's `runtime` dependencies become `runtime` for you, and `test`/`provided` ones are not inherited at all.

Prefer fixed versions. Version ranges (`[1.2,2.0)`) make builds non-reproducible. Keep versions in `<properties>` (`<junit.version>5.11.4</junit.version>`) or in `dependencyManagement` so they're declared once.
concepts.code:
<properties>
  <junit.version>5.11.4</junit.version>
</properties>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>                               <!-- compile scope (default) -->
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.18.3</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>                               <!-- only at run time -->
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <version>42.7.5</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>                               <!-- compile-time only, not packaged -->
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
    <version>1.18.36</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>${junit.version}</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
<!-- mvn dependency:tree      mvn dependency:analyze -->
takeaways: compile is the default and propagates to consumers
provided and runtime split compile-time from run-time needs
test scope keeps test libraries out of the artifact
dependency:tree and dependency:analyze inspect the graph
pitfalls: Declaring a JDBC driver with compile scope and accidentally coding against driver-specific classes.

quiz.q: Which scope should the JUnit library have?
quiz.explain: JUnit is only needed to compile and run tests, so test scope keeps it out of the shipped artifact.

concepts.name: The build lifecycle
concepts.summary: Understand phases, how plugins' goals bind to them, and what mvn verify or mvn install actually runs.
concepts.why: Knowing which goals run in which phase explains why tests run on package and how to hook in extra steps.
concepts.body:
Maven has three built-in **lifecycles**: `default` (build), `clean` and `site`. A lifecycle is an ordered list of **phases**. Running a phase runs it and every phase before it. The main phases of `default`:

1. `validate`
2. `compile` (compiles `src/main/java`)
3. `test-compile`, then `test` (runs unit tests with the **Surefire** plugin)
4. `package` (builds the jar/war with the **Jar** plugin)
5. `integration-test` and `verify` (**Failsafe** runs integration tests named `*IT`)
6. `install` (copies to `~/.m2`)
7. `deploy` (uploads to a remote repository)

So `mvn package` compiles, runs tests and builds the jar; `mvn install` additionally installs it. `mvn clean install` first runs the `clean` lifecycle.

Phases do nothing themselves. Work is done by **plugin goals** such as `compiler:compile`, `surefire:test` or `jar:jar`, which the packaging type binds to phases by default. You can run a goal directly without the lifecycle: `mvn dependency:tree`, `mvn versions:display-dependency-updates`, `mvn help:effective-pom` (shows the POM after inheritance and defaults).

Bind extra goals to phases in `<build><plugins>` with an `<executions>` block, for example running a code generator in `generate-sources` or Failsafe in `integration-test`.

`-DskipTests` compiles tests but doesn't run them; `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` skips compiling them too.
concepts.code:
# Each phase runs all earlier phases
mvn compile             # validate -> compile
mvn test                # ... -> test-compile -> test      (Surefire)
mvn package             # ... -> package                   (Jar plugin)
mvn verify              # ... -> integration-test -> verify (Failsafe)
mvn install             # ... -> install  (~/.m2/repository)
mvn clean install       # clean lifecycle first, then default up to install

# Goals can be invoked directly, outside the lifecycle
mvn help:effective-pom          # POM after inheritance and defaults
mvn dependency:tree
mvn surefire:test -Dtest=UserServiceTest
mvn versions:display-dependency-updates

# Skipping tests
mvn package -DskipTests          # compile tests but don't run
mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true   # don't even compile them
takeaways: A phase runs every phase before it
Plugins' goals are bound to phases; packaging sets the defaults
verify includes Failsafe integration tests; install copies to ~/.m2
plugin:goal runs a goal directly

quiz.q: What runs when you execute mvn package?
options: All phases up to package, including compile and test
Only compile and package, tests are skipped
quiz.explain: Phases are cumulative: package runs validate, compile, test-compile, test and then package.

concepts.name: Testing with Surefire and Failsafe
concepts.summary: Run JUnit 5 unit tests with Surefire, integration tests with Failsafe, and filter or configure test runs.
concepts.why: Test execution is where most day-to-day Maven interaction happens.
concepts.body:
The **Surefire** plugin runs unit tests in the `test` phase. It picks up classes named `*Test`, `Test*`, `*Tests` or `*TestCase` from `src/test/java`. For JUnit 5, add `org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter` with test scope; Surefire 3.x detects the JUnit Platform automatically. Pin the Surefire version in `<build><plugins>` (or a parent) because the default bound version may be old.

Filtering and options:

- `mvn test -Dtest=UserServiceTest` or `-Dtest='User*Test#create*'` for a class or methods.
- `-Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false` when a filter matches nothing in some modules.
- `-DskipTests` to skip; `-Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true` to continue despite failures.
- Configure JVM args, system properties, parallelism (`<forkCount>`, `<parallel>`) and includes/excludes in the plugin's `<configuration>`.

Reports go to `target/surefire-reports/` (text and JUnit XML for CI).

**Failsafe** is Surefire's sibling for integration tests. It runs `*IT` classes in the `integration-test` phase and only fails the build in `verify`, so a `post-integration-test` phase can still tear down containers or servers. You must add it explicitly with executions for `integration-test` and `verify`. Run `mvn verify` to include it.

Test output is captured by default; set `<redirectTestOutputToFile>` or use `-Dsurefire.printSummary` and look in the reports when debugging.
concepts.code:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.2</version>
      <configuration>
        <excludedGroups>slow</excludedGroups>         <!-- JUnit 5 @Tag("slow") -->
        <systemPropertyVariables>
          <app.env>test</app.env>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.2</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals><goal>integration-test</goal><goal>verify</goal></goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
<!-- mvn test -Dtest=UserServiceTest        -> unit tests only
     mvn verify                             -> unit tests + *IT integration tests
     reports: target/surefire-reports, target/failsafe-reports -->
takeaways: Surefire runs *Test classes in the test phase
Failsafe runs *IT classes in integration-test and fails in verify
-Dtest=Class#method filters; -DskipTests skips
Reports land in target/surefire-reports
pitfalls: Naming an integration test *Test, so it runs with the fast unit tests on every mvn test.

quiz.q: Why does Failsafe fail the build in verify rather than in integration-test?
options: So post-integration-test can still run cleanup before the build fails
quiz.explain: Deferring the failure lets teardown goals bound to post-integration-test run first.

concepts.name: dependencyManagement and BOMs
concepts.summary: Centralize versions with dependencyManagement, import BOMs, and understand how managed versions apply to transitives.
concepts.why: This is how Spring Boot and large projects keep hundreds of dependency versions consistent.
concepts.body:
`<dependencyManagement>` declares versions (and scopes, exclusions) **without adding** the dependencies. Modules or the `<dependencies>` section then list only `groupId` and `artifactId`, inheriting the managed version. Managed versions also apply to **transitive** dependencies, so declaring `jackson-databind` there pins the version wherever it appears in the graph.

A **BOM** (bill of materials) is a POM with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` containing only a `dependencyManagement` section. Import it with scope `import`:

```xml
<dependencyManagement><dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.4</version>
    <type>pom</type>
    <scope>import</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies></dependencyManagement>
```

After that, Spring, Jackson, JUnit and dozens of other libraries can be declared without versions and are guaranteed to be mutually compatible. Spring Boot projects more often inherit from `spring-boot-starter-parent`, which imports this BOM and also configures plugins; importing the BOM is the alternative when you need your own parent.

Precedence: a version declared directly in `<dependencies>` beats a managed one; among managed versions, the first declaration in the POM (including the order of imported BOMs) wins. Use `mvn help:effective-pom` to see the final result and `mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose` to see which versions were managed.
concepts.code:
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>                                       <!-- import a BOM -->
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.4</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>                                       <!-- pin a version everywhere -->
      <groupId>com.google.guava</groupId>
      <artifactId>guava</artifactId>
      <version>33.4.0-jre</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>                                         <!-- versions come from management -->
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.guava</groupId>
    <artifactId>guava</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
takeaways: dependencyManagement sets versions without adding dependencies
Managed versions also override transitive versions
Import a BOM with type pom and scope import
Direct versions beat managed ones; first managed declaration wins

quiz.q: What happens if a dependency is listed in dependencyManagement but not in dependencies?
options: It is added with compile scope
Nothing is added; only its version is fixed if it appears anywhere in the graph
It is added with test scope
quiz.explain: dependencyManagement only manages versions and settings; it never adds a dependency by itself.

concepts.name: Configuring plugins
concepts.summary: Configure plugins in the build section, bind executions to phases, and use pluginManagement for shared settings.
concepts.why: Compiler flags, packaging, code generation and quality checks are all plugin configuration.
concepts.body:
Plugins are declared under `<build><plugins>` with coordinates and a `<configuration>` block. Maven's plugins (`org.apache.maven.plugins` group) can omit the groupId. Always pin plugin versions; otherwise Maven warns and picks a possibly outdated default.

Key plugins:

- **maven-compiler-plugin**: `<release>21</release>`, `<compilerArgs>`, `<annotationProcessorPaths>` for Lombok or MapStruct.
- **maven-jar-plugin**: manifest entries such as `Main-Class`.
- **maven-shade-plugin** or **spring-boot-maven-plugin**: build a runnable fat jar.
- **maven-enforcer-plugin**: require a Maven/JDK version, ban duplicate or snapshot dependencies.
- **maven-resources-plugin** with `<filtering>true</filtering>` substitutes `${project.version}` in resource files.
- **exec-maven-plugin**, **build-helper-maven-plugin**, **jacoco-maven-plugin**, **spotless-maven-plugin**.

An `<execution>` binds goals to a phase, with its own `<id>` and configuration; the same plugin can have several executions. Omit `<phase>` when the goal has a default phase. Run a single execution directly with `mvn plugin:goal@executionId`.

`<pluginManagement>` works like `dependencyManagement`: it fixes versions and configuration for plugins without activating them, so child modules just name the plugin. Put it in the parent POM.

Configuration values can reference properties (`${java.version}`) and be overridden from the command line with `-Dproperty=value` only when the plugin exposes a user property (documented per goal, e.g. `-Dmaven.compiler.release=17`).
concepts.code:
<build>
  <pluginManagement>                         <!-- versions/config for the whole build -->
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.13.0</version>
        <configuration>
          <release>21</release>
          <compilerArgs><arg>-Xlint:all</arg></compilerArgs>
        </configuration>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </pluginManagement>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-enforcer-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.0</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <id>enforce-versions</id>
          <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>     <!-- default phase: validate -->
          <configuration>
            <rules>
              <requireMavenVersion><version>[3.9,)</version></requireMavenVersion>
              <requireJavaVersion><version>[21,)</version></requireJavaVersion>
              <banDuplicatePomDependencyVersions/>
            </rules>
          </configuration>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
takeaways: Pin plugin versions under build/plugins or pluginManagement
executions bind goals to phases with their own configuration
pluginManagement shares settings without activating plugins
Compiler, surefire, jar/shade and enforcer are the core set
pitfalls: Leaving plugin versions unspecified, so builds change behavior when Maven's defaults change.

quiz.q: What is the difference between plugins and pluginManagement?
options: plugins is for parents, pluginManagement for children
pluginManagement only sets versions and configuration; plugins actually adds the plugin to the build
quiz.explain: Like dependencyManagement, pluginManagement is declarative; the plugin runs only where it is listed under plugins.

concepts.name: Multi-module projects and parent POMs
concepts.summary: Structure a build as a parent POM with modules, share configuration through inheritance, and build selected modules.
concepts.why: Most real Maven codebases are multi-module; inheritance and the reactor are what make them manageable.
concepts.body:
A **multi-module** build has a root POM with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` that lists `<modules>` (folder names). Each module has its own POM and usually declares the root as its `<parent>`. Two separate mechanisms are at work:

- **Aggregation** (`<modules>`): the **reactor** builds all listed modules, ordering them by their inter-dependencies.
- **Inheritance** (`<parent>`): a child POM inherits properties, `dependencyManagement`, `pluginManagement`, repositories and plugins from its parent. The child needs only `artifactId` (groupId and version are inherited). `<relativePath>` points to the parent POM on disk; the default `../pom.xml` works for the usual layout.

Modules depend on each other with normal `<dependency>` elements using `${project.version}` for the version. The reactor resolves these from the modules being built (in Maven 3, the artifact must have been packaged in the same run, which is why `mvn install` was the traditional command; Maven 4 handles this better).

Useful reactor flags:

- `-pl api,core` build selected modules; `-am` also build their dependencies; `-amd` also build dependents.
- `-rf :api` resume from a module after a failure.
- `-T 4` (or `-T 1C`) builds independent modules in parallel.

Keep versions in sync across modules with the **flatten** or **versions** plugins, or with `${revision}` **CI-friendly versions** (`<version>${revision}</version>` and `-Drevision=1.2.0`).

Run `mvn help:effective-pom -pl api` to see what a module really inherits.
concepts.code:
<!-- pom.xml (root / parent) -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  <version>${revision}</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>
  <properties>
    <revision>1.2.0-SNAPSHOT</revision>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
  </properties>
  <modules>
    <module>core</module>
    <module>api</module>
  </modules>
</project>
<!-- api/pom.xml -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <parent>
    <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
    <version>${revision}</version>
  </parent>
  <artifactId>api</artifactId>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
      <artifactId>core</artifactId>
      <version>${project.version}</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
<!-- mvn -pl api -am package     mvn -T 1C verify     mvn -rf :api install -->
takeaways: modules aggregate (reactor); parent inherits (configuration)
Children inherit groupId, version, management sections and plugins
-pl, -am, -amd and -rf select what to build; -T parallelizes
Use ${revision} or the flatten plugin for CI-friendly versions
pitfalls: Changing the parent version and forgetting to update the <parent> block in every module.

quiz.q: What does mvn -pl api -am package do?
options: Builds api and every module it depends on
Builds api and every module that depends on it
quiz.explain: -am (also-make) adds the selected module's upstream dependencies to the reactor.

concepts.name: Profiles, properties and settings.xml
concepts.summary: Vary the build per environment with profiles, properties and the user-level settings.xml for mirrors and credentials.
concepts.why: CI servers, private repositories and environment-specific builds all rely on profiles and settings.
concepts.body:
**Properties** are placeholders used throughout the POM: `${project.version}`, `${project.basedir}`, environment variables `${env.HOME}`, system properties, and your own from `<properties>`. Override them from the command line with `-Dname=value`.

**Profiles** are blocks of POM configuration applied conditionally. A profile can add dependencies, plugins, properties and modules. Activate one:

- Explicitly: `mvn package -Pprod` (or `-P!prod` to deactivate).
- By property: `<activation><property><name>env</name><value>ci</value></property></activation>` matches `-Denv=ci`.
- By JDK, OS, or a file's existence; or `<activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>`, which is switched off as soon as any other profile is active (a common surprise).

`mvn help:active-profiles` lists what is active. Don't use profiles to produce different artifacts from the same version (a "prod jar" and a "dev jar" with the same coordinates); keep environment config outside the artifact.

**settings.xml** (`~/.m2/settings.xml`, or `$MAVEN_HOME/conf` globally) is personal and machine-specific, never committed:

- `<mirrors>` redirect all repository traffic to a company proxy such as Nexus or Artifactory.
- `<servers>` hold credentials for deploying or for private repositories, matched by `<id>`; encrypt passwords with `mvn --encrypt-password`.
- `<profiles>` and `<activeProfiles>` for local defaults; `<proxies>` for HTTP proxies.

CI typically supplies a settings file with `mvn -s ci-settings.xml` and credentials from environment variables (`${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}`).
concepts.code:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>ci</id>
    <activation>
      <property><name>env</name><value>ci</value></property>   <!-- mvn -Denv=ci -->
    </activation>
    <properties>
      <skipITs>false</skipITs>
    </properties>
  </profile>
  <profile>
    <id>jdk-preview</id>
    <activation><jdk>[25,)</jdk></activation>
    <properties><maven.compiler.enablePreview>true</maven.compiler.enablePreview></properties>
  </profile>
</profiles>
<!-- ~/.m2/settings.xml (not committed) -->
<settings>
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>nexus</id>
      <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
      <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
    </mirror>
  </mirrors>
  <servers>
    <server><id>nexus</id><username>ci</username><password>${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}</password></server>
  </servers>
</settings>
<!-- mvn verify -Pci        mvn help:active-profiles -->
takeaways: Properties parameterize the POM; override with -Dname=value
Profiles add configuration conditionally (-P, properties, JDK, OS)
activeByDefault switches off when another profile is active
settings.xml holds mirrors and credentials and stays uncommitted
pitfalls: Baking environment-specific values into the artifact through profiles, producing jars that differ by build machine.

quiz.q: A profile is activeByDefault. You run mvn package -Pci. Is the default profile still active?
options: No: activeByDefault profiles are deactivated when any other profile is explicitly activated
quiz.explain: activeByDefault means 'active unless another profile in the same POM is active', a frequent surprise.

concepts.name: Transitive conflicts and exclusions
concepts.summary: Understand nearest-wins resolution, read dependency:tree output, and fix conflicts with exclusions and managed versions.
concepts.why: Classpath conflicts cause NoSuchMethodError at run time; diagnosing them is a core Maven skill.
concepts.body:
When the same library is reachable through several paths, Maven's **nearest-wins** (dependency mediation) rule picks the version whose path from your POM is shortest; for equal depth, the first declaration wins. This can silently select an *older* version than another path needs, leading to `NoSuchMethodError` or `ClassNotFoundException` at run time.

Diagnosing:

- `mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose` shows omitted versions and why (`omitted for conflict with 2.18.3`).
- `mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core` narrows the output.
- `mvn dependency:analyze` finds undeclared and unused dependencies.
- `mvn dependency:list -DoutputFile=...` for scripting.

Fixing:

- **Manage** the version in `dependencyManagement`: it applies to all paths, the cleanest fix.
- **Exclude** a transitive dependency on a specific path: `<exclusions><exclusion><groupId>..</groupId><artifactId>..</artifactId></exclusion></exclusions>`, for example removing `commons-logging` in favor of `jcl-over-slf4j`, or an old `log4j`.
- Declare the dependency directly (depth 1) to force it nearest; prefer management over this trick.
- `<optional>true</optional>` on your own dependency stops it from propagating to consumers.

Watch for **duplicate classes** from relocated artifacts (`javax.*` vs `jakarta.*`, `commons-lang` vs `commons-lang3`), which no mediation can solve; the **enforcer** plugin's `banDuplicateClasses` (from extra-enforcer-rules) and `dependencyConvergence` rules catch these in CI.
concepts.code:
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId>
    <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId>
    <version>5.4.3</version>
    <exclusions>
      <exclusion>                              <!-- drop a transitive on this path -->
        <groupId>commons-logging</groupId>
        <artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>
      </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>jcl-over-slf4j</artifactId>   <!-- bridge replacing it -->
    <version>2.0.17</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- $ mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core
[INFO] com.acme:shop-api:jar:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.18.3:compile
[INFO] \- com.example:legacy-lib:jar:1.0:compile
[INFO]    \- (com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.12.7:compile
             - omitted for conflict with 2.18.3)
   Fix for the other direction (an old version winning): pin it in dependencyManagement. -->
takeaways: Nearest path wins, then first declaration; not the highest version
dependency:tree -Dverbose shows omitted versions and why
Fix with dependencyManagement first, exclusions second
Enforcer rules catch convergence and duplicate-class problems in CI
pitfalls: Excluding a transitive dependency that the library actually needs, moving the failure to run time.

quiz.q: Your POM depends on A (which needs X 1.0) and B (which needs C, which needs X 2.0). Which X does Maven select?
options: X 1.0, because its path is shorter
quiz.explain: Maven's nearest-wins rule picks the version with the shortest path, X 1.0 via A.

concepts.name: Packaging runnable applications
concepts.summary: Build executable jars with the jar, shade or Spring Boot plugins, handle resources and manifests, and avoid shading pitfalls.
concepts.why: Shipping a service means producing something that runs with java -jar; each approach has trade-offs.
concepts.body:
A plain `mvn package` jar contains only your classes; dependencies are not included and the manifest has no `Main-Class`. Options for runnable artifacts:

- **Jar plugin + classpath**: set `<manifest><mainClass>` and `<addClasspath>true</addClasspath>`, and copy dependencies next to it with `dependency:copy-dependencies`. Clean and fast, but you ship a folder.
- **maven-shade-plugin**: merges all dependency classes into one **uber jar** (`java -jar app.jar`). Use the `ManifestResourceTransformer` for `Main-Class` and `ServicesResourceTransformer` to merge `META-INF/services` files, or service loading (JDBC drivers, Jackson modules) silently breaks. Shade can also **relocate** packages to avoid conflicts, which is how libraries bundle dependencies safely. Signed jars must have their signatures excluded.
- **maven-assembly-plugin** with the `jar-with-dependencies` descriptor: simpler but merges files naively.
- **spring-boot-maven-plugin** `repackage`: nests dependency jars inside a launcher jar, avoiding merging problems; also builds OCI images with `build-image`.
- **jlink/jpackage** plugins produce custom runtimes and native installers.

Resources from `src/main/resources` are copied into the jar; enable `<filtering>` to inject `${project.version}` into files like `application.properties`, but keep binaries out of filtered directories.

Set `project.build.outputTimestamp` for **reproducible builds** so the same source yields a byte-identical jar, which the Maven Release and verification tooling increasingly expect.
concepts.code:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.6.0</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <phase>package</phase>
          <goals><goal>shade</goal></goals>
          <configuration>
            <createDependencyReducedPom>false</createDependencyReducedPom>
            <transformers>
              <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer">
                <mainClass>com.acme.App</mainClass>
              </transformer>
              <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ServicesResourceTransformer"/>
            </transformers>
            <filters>
              <filter>                     <!-- drop signatures of signed dependencies -->
                <artifact>*:*</artifact>
                <excludes><exclude>META-INF/*.SF</exclude><exclude>META-INF/*.DSA</exclude><exclude>META-INF/*.RSA</exclude></excludes>
              </filter>
            </filters>
          </configuration>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
<!-- mvn package && java -jar target/shop-api-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar -->
takeaways: A default jar has no dependencies and no Main-Class
Shade merges classes; use transformers for manifests and META-INF/services
Spring Boot's repackage nests jars instead of merging
Set project.build.outputTimestamp for reproducible jars
pitfalls: Shading without ServicesResourceTransformer, so JDBC drivers or Jackson modules are not found at run time.

quiz.q: Why can a shaded jar fail to find a JDBC driver that works in the IDE?
options: META-INF/services files from several jars overwrote each other instead of being merged
The driver must be provided scope
quiz.explain: Service loader registrations live in identically named files; without the services transformer only one survives.

concepts.name: Deploying and releasing artifacts
concepts.summary: Publish snapshots and releases to repositories with distributionManagement, the deploy plugin, versions plugin and release flows.
concepts.why: Sharing libraries across teams and publishing to Maven Central is a core Maven workflow.
concepts.body:
`mvn deploy` uploads the artifact, its POM and attached artifacts (sources, javadoc) to the repository in `<distributionManagement>`. Credentials come from a `<server>` in `settings.xml` whose `<id>` matches.

Snapshots vs releases:

- A `-SNAPSHOT` version can be deployed repeatedly; each upload gets a timestamp and consumers re-check for newer ones (daily by default, `-U` forces an update). Snapshot repositories are for ongoing work.
- A **release** version is immutable; repositories reject re-uploads. Releases must not depend on snapshots (the enforcer's `requireReleaseDeps` checks this).

Releasing means: set the release version, tag, build and deploy, then bump to the next snapshot. Tools:

- `versions:set -DnewVersion=1.3.0` and `versions:commit`, scripted in CI; with `${revision}` CI-friendly versions you simply pass `-Drevision=1.3.0` and use the **flatten** plugin so the deployed POM has a concrete version.
- **maven-release-plugin** (`release:prepare` and `release:perform`) automates the tag-and-bump cycle, with more ceremony.

**Maven Central** publishing goes through Sonatype's Central Portal (`central-publishing-maven-plugin`) and requires a verified namespace, source and javadoc jars (`maven-source-plugin`, `maven-javadoc-plugin`), full POM metadata (name, description, url, license, developers, scm) and GPG signatures (`maven-gpg-plugin`).

Attach sources with the `jar-no-fork` goal so they're deployed alongside the main jar. Never deploy from a dirty working tree or with local uncommitted changes.
concepts.code:
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>nexus</id>                                  <!-- matches <server id="nexus"> in settings.xml -->
    <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-releases/</url>
  </repository>
  <snapshotRepository>
    <id>nexus</id>
    <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-snapshots/</url>
  </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-source-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.3.1</version>
      <executions>
        <execution><id>sources</id><goals><goal>jar-no-fork</goal></goals></execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

<!-- Snapshot:  mvn deploy                       (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT, repeatable)
     Release:   mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=1.3.0 && mvn versions:commit
                mvn -DskipTests deploy && git tag v1.3.0
                mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=1.4.0-SNAPSHOT
     or with CI-friendly versions: mvn -Drevision=1.3.0 deploy -->
takeaways: mvn deploy uploads to distributionManagement using settings.xml credentials
Snapshots are mutable and re-checked; releases are immutable
Release = set version, tag, deploy, bump to next snapshot
Central requires sources, javadoc, POM metadata and GPG signatures
pitfalls: Releasing a version that still depends on a -SNAPSHOT library, which later disappears or changes.

quiz.q: Why does a repository reject a second mvn deploy of version 1.3.0?
options: Release versions are immutable; only -SNAPSHOT versions may be redeployed
Deploy only works once per day
quiz.explain: Consumers rely on a release version always meaning the same bytes, so repositories refuse to overwrite it.

concepts.name: Writing Maven plugins and extensions
concepts.summary: Write a Mojo with annotated parameters, bind it to a phase, test it, and know when a core extension is the right tool.
concepts.why: Custom plugins encode organization-specific build steps; understanding Mojos also demystifies every plugin you configure.
concepts.body:
A Maven plugin is a jar with packaging `maven-plugin` containing **Mojos** (Maven plain Old Java Objects): classes annotated with `@Mojo(name = "goal", defaultPhase = LifecyclePhase.X)` that extend `AbstractMojo` and implement `execute()`.

Parameters are fields annotated with `@Parameter(property = "greeting.name", defaultValue = "World")`. Users configure them in `<configuration>` or via `-Dgreeting.name=Ada`. Inject build context with `@Parameter(defaultValue = "${project}", readonly = true) MavenProject project`, or `${session}`, `${mojoExecution}`. Components such as the repository system are injected with `@Inject` (or the older `@Component`).

Mojo flags: `requiresDependencyResolution = ResolutionScope.COMPILE` to get the resolved classpath, `threadSafe = true` for `-T` builds, `aggregator = true` to run once at the root of a reactor.

The `maven-plugin-plugin` generates the plugin descriptor (`META-INF/maven/plugin.xml`) from the annotations at build time. Users apply the plugin like any other, by coordinates; a `<pluginGroup>` in settings lets them use the short `prefix:goal` form.

Testing: `maven-plugin-testing-harness` for unit tests, and **maven-invoker-plugin** to run real sample projects under `src/it` as integration tests. Log with `getLog()`, fail with `MojoFailureException` (build problem) or `MojoExecutionException` (unexpected error).

**Core extensions** (`.mvn/extensions.xml`) hook into Maven itself rather than the lifecycle: CI-friendly versioning (`maven-git-versioning-extension`), build caching (`maven-build-cache-extension`), or Develocity/Gradle Enterprise build scans. Maven 4 keeps the plugin API largely compatible (`org.apache.maven.api` offers a new one), so plugins written this way keep working.
takeaways: A Mojo is an annotated class with execute(); @Parameter fields are its configuration
defaultPhase binds the goal; ${project} and @Inject give build context
Test with the plugin testing harness and invoker integration tests
Core extensions hook into Maven itself (caching, versioning)

quiz.q: How does Maven know which phase a goal runs in when the user doesn't specify <phase>?
options: It runs immediately at configuration time
From the Mojo's defaultPhase in the generated plugin descriptor
quiz.explain: The maven-plugin-plugin writes defaultPhase into plugin.xml, which Maven reads to bind the goal.

concepts.name: Build performance and reproducibility
concepts.summary: Speed up Maven with parallel builds, the daemon, build cache extension and incremental compilation, and make builds reproducible.
concepts.why: Slow and non-deterministic builds hurt CI and trust; Maven has specific remedies for both.
concepts.body:
Maven builds are often slower than they need to be. Levers, roughly in order of payoff:

- **Parallel reactor**: `-T 1C` builds independent modules concurrently (one thread per core). Plugins must be marked thread-safe; Maven warns about the rest.
- **mvnd** (the Maven Daemon): a long-running, warmed-up JVM with a native client that cuts startup from seconds to milliseconds and runs modules in parallel by default. Maven 4 integrates these ideas.
- **maven-build-cache-extension**: caches module outputs keyed by inputs (sources, POM, dependencies), locally or in a remote store, so unchanged modules are restored rather than rebuilt. Add it in `.mvn/extensions.xml` and tune `maven-build-cache-config.xml`.
- Skip what you don't need: `-DskipTests` for local packaging, `-o` offline when the local repo is warm, `-pl`/`-am` for a subset, `-Dmaven.javadoc.skip`.
- Reduce plugin executions: enforcer, checkstyle and site generation can run in a separate CI job. Use `-Dmaven.test.redirectTestOutputToFile=true` and Surefire forking tuned for your machine.
- Check what's slow with `-Dorg.slf4j.simpleLogger.showDateTime=true` or a profiler extension (`maven-profiler`).

**Reproducible builds**: with `project.build.outputTimestamp` set (`<project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>`, updated at release), the jar, source and javadoc plugins normalize file timestamps and ordering so the same inputs give byte-identical artifacts. Pin every plugin version, avoid version ranges and `LATEST`, and use the **dependency lock** approach of a BOM plus enforcer `requireUpperBoundDeps`/`dependencyConvergence` to keep resolution stable. `artifact:compare` (maven-artifact-plugin) verifies reproducibility against a reference build.

CI tips: cache `~/.m2/repository`, use the wrapper, pass `--batch-mode` and `--no-transfer-progress`.
concepts.code:
# .mvn/maven.config  (defaults applied to every mvn invocation in this repo)
--batch-mode
--no-transfer-progress
-T 1C

# .mvn/extensions.xml
# <extensions>
#   <extension>
#     <groupId>org.apache.maven.extensions</groupId>
#     <artifactId>maven-build-cache-extension</artifactId>
#     <version>1.2.0</version>
#   </extension>
# </extensions>

# pom.xml property for reproducible archives
# <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>

mvnd verify                                  # Maven Daemon: warm JVM, parallel by default
mvn -o -pl api -am -DskipTests package       # offline, subset of modules
mvn verify -Dmaven.build.cache.enabled=true  # with the cache extension installed
mvn clean verify artifact:compare            # check the build is reproducible
# CI: cache ~/.m2/repository between runs; always use ./mvnw
takeaways: -T 1C and mvnd parallelize and remove JVM startup cost
The build cache extension restores unchanged modules
project.build.outputTimestamp plus pinned versions give byte-identical builds
Cache ~/.m2 and use --batch-mode in CI
pitfalls: Enabling -T with plugins that aren't thread-safe and getting intermittent build failures.

options: Reproducible archives: identical bytes for identical inputs
quiz.explain: It makes the archiver normalize entry timestamps and ordering so repeated builds produce the same jar.

concepts.name: Maven 4: what changes
concepts.summary: Know the Maven 4 changes: model version 4.1.0, build vs consumer POMs, subprojects, reactor improvements and the new API.
concepts.why: Maven 4 is the first major release in a decade; teams maintaining builds need to know what to adopt.
concepts.body:
Maven 4 (released after a long 4.0 beta cycle) keeps Maven 3 POMs building but modernizes the core:

- **Model 4.1.0**: a new POM schema. Children can omit the parent `version` and `groupId`, and `<subprojects>` replaces `<modules>` (both still work). Maven 3 users can keep model 4.0.0.
- **Build POM vs consumer POM**: the POM you write (with `${revision}`, parent relativePath, build plugins) is transformed on install/deploy into a lean **consumer POM** with resolved versions and no build details. This makes CI-friendly versions work without the flatten plugin.
- **Reactor improvements**: modules resolve against each other from `target/classes` more reliably, so `mvn verify` works across modules without `install`; `-r`/`--resume` resumes a failed build automatically; `-pl` accepts `:artifactId` paths and the reactor validates missing modules.
- **Parallel and daemon**: `-T` is more robust, and the mvnd daemon is being merged in.
- **Stricter and clearer**: deprecated options and plugins fail or warn earlier (e.g. `system` scope, `LATEST`/`RELEASE` versions, missing plugin versions), and error messages are improved.
- **New API** (`org.apache.maven.api.*`) for plugins and extensions, immutable and with proper lifecycle and session objects; the Maven 3 API is still supported for compatibility.
- Requires Java 17 to run (projects can still target older bytecode).

Adoption path: upgrade the wrapper to a 4.x distribution, run the build, fix warnings about plugin versions and deprecated features, then migrate to model 4.1.0 and `<subprojects>` once all contributors are on Maven 4. Check plugin compatibility notes; most mainstream plugins already support Maven 4.
concepts.code:
<!-- Maven 4 POM using model 4.1.0 -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.1.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  <version>1.2.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>

  <subprojects>                      <!-- replaces <modules> -->
    <subproject>core</subproject>
    <subproject>api</subproject>
  </subprojects>
</project>

<!-- api/pom.xml: parent version and groupId can be omitted -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0">
  <modelVersion>4.1.0</modelVersion>
  <parent>
    <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  </parent>
  <artifactId>api</artifactId>
</project>

<!-- ./mvnw wrapper:wrapper -Dmaven=4.0.0   then:  ./mvnw verify  (no install needed across modules) -->
takeaways: Model 4.1.0 adds <subprojects> and optional parent version/groupId
Build POM vs consumer POM makes ${revision} versions clean
Reactor builds work across modules without install
New immutable API for plugins; Maven 3 API still supported

quiz.q: What is the consumer POM in Maven 4?
options: A POM that lists who uses your library
A simplified POM with resolved versions and no build details, generated at install/deploy
quiz.explain: Maven 4 transforms the build POM into a lean consumer POM so downstream resolution is simple and stable.
